activities.title: The staging step
activities.instruction: Understand staging as an explicit choice about what belongs in the next commit, and commits as deliberate saved points in project history.

content.title: Stage a Change, Then Commit It
content.context:
```text
src/cart.js
README.md
```

But you only want the cart behavior change in the next saved version.

Git gives you a staging area so you can choose which changes belong together.

A simplified flow is:

```text
working tree
     ↓
choose changes
     ↓
staging area
     ↓
commit
     ↓
recorded history
```
goals: Understand staging as an explicit choice about what belongs in the next commit, and commits as deliberate saved points in project history.

content.title: Stage one file
content.text:
You can stage one specific file with:

```bash
git add src/cart.js
```

Now the cart change is selected for the next commit.

The README change remains unstaged.

content.question: After staging only `src/cart.js`, which statement is correct?

options.text: The cart change is selected for the next commit; the README change remains outside that commit.

feedback.correct: Staging is selection. It does not delete other changes or commit anything by itself.
feedback.incorrect: Staging is selection. It does not delete other changes or commit anything by itself.

content.title: Inspect the staged idea
content.text:
A useful habit is:

```bash
git diff
```

for ordinary working-tree differences, and then inspect the staged changes before committing.

Conceptually, ask two questions:

1. **What changed?**
2. **What am I about to record?**

Those questions prevent a surprising number of bad commits.

content.title: Make a focused commit
content.text:
A commit should describe one coherent change.

Good example:

```text
Fix cart total when quantity changes
```

Weak example:

```text
stuff
```

The goal is not literary beauty. The goal is future clarity.

Six weeks from now, another engineer should be able to understand why that snapshot exists.

content.title: Commit the staged work
content.text:
After reviewing the staged changes, the conceptual action is:

```bash
git commit -m "Fix cart total when quantity changes"
```

The commit records the staged selection as a new point in project history.

content.question:
You discover that your working tree contains:

```text
src/cart.js          → fixes quantity calculation
README.md            → rewrites unrelated instructions
notes/debug.txt      → your temporary scratch notes
```

Would you put all three into one commit?

options.text: Yes. Git works best when commits are large.
No. Separate unrelated work so the history tells a clearer story.
Only the scratch notes should be committed.

feedback.correct: Focused commits make review, reasoning, and recovery easier.
feedback.incorrect: Focused commits make review, reasoning, and recovery easier.

guidelines: State your reasoning clearly in your own words or code.

content.title: Forge takeaway & Lesson completion
takeaways: **Mental model:** Staging is selection. A commit is a deliberate saved point.
**Senior habit:** Never commit blindly. Read the change you are about to record.
nextSteps: Explain why staging and committing are separate steps.
